summary: For ages 5–7, build the idea that wind is moving air — invisible itself, but known by what it does (leaves swirl, flags snap, hair blows, it pushes you) — and that wind has a strength spectrum from gentle breeze to strong gale. Confront the intuition that 'air is nothing' by showing air is real stuff that can push. Keep the CAUSE of wind (uneven heating/rising air) out at this age; that is a later 7–9 topic. Ground learning in first-hand experience (blowing, fanning, a windy-day walk) before any screen model.
misconceptions: 'Wind is made by trees waving' (or fans/clouds) — reversed cause: the moving air makes the trees wave, not the other way round.
'Air is nothing / empty' — wind demonstrates air is real matter that can push objects and be felt.
'Wind blows because the weather is angry / on purpose' — animistic framing; keep it to observation, defer real cause.
'Windy always means cold' — wind can be warm or cold; strength and temperature are separate.
'You can see the wind' — we see its EFFECTS and things it carries, not the moving air itself.

activities.title: Make your own wind
steps: Blow on the back of your own hand and feel the push.
Wave a hand or a fan at your face and feel the moving air.
Wave a streamer or strip of paper and watch it flutter in the air you move.
Talk about where outdoor wind is the same idea (moving air) but comes from outside rather than from you.
Indoors with the windows shut, work out how you could still make a little wind yourself (blow, fan, wave) — showing wind is just air moving, not something from a single fixed source.
activities.insight: Air is real stuff you can feel, and wind is simply air that is moving. You can make moving air yourself with your breath or a fan — the same idea as outdoor wind, just a different source.

activities.title: Crank the wind from breeze to gale
steps: Use a wind-strength control (e.g. a slider or dial) that goes from gentle breeze up to strong gale, coupled to an outdoor scene that responds live.
Nudge the strength up a little and watch a few leaves stir and a flag ripple — name this a breeze.
Push the strength higher and watch branches sway, a kite lift and pull on its string, and hair stream sideways.
Push to the top and watch the whole tree bend, a hat tumble off and roll away, and a character lean hard into the gust to keep walking — name this a gale.
Drag objects into the scene and test 'can the wind move this?' — compare a leaf (blows away) with a heavy rock (stays put).
Read a windsock or flag whose angle leans further as the strength increases, showing the invisible wind's strength and direction.
activities.insight: Wind is moving air: you never see the air itself, only what it does. By changing the strength yourself in the model, you see wind as moving air of varying strength — a spectrum from breeze to gale — recognised by its effects, and you can link this to how real wind has felt on your body.

activities.title: Which way does the cause go? (trees and wind)
steps: Look at or imagine a windy day with tree branches waving about.
Consider a claim: 'The trees are making the wind by waving.' Decide whether it is right and explain why.
Compare a windless day where nothing waves with a fan (moving air) making a still branch wave — notice the moving air moves the branch.
State in your own words what wind actually is and what is really happening with the trees.
activities.insight: Wind is moving air, and the moving air pushes the branches, which is why they wave — the trees do not make the wind. Cause goes from moving air to moving object, not the reverse.

activities.title: Sort and order by what wind does
steps: Sort objects into 'the wind can move this easily' (kite, leaves, flag, hat, washing) versus 'the wind can't easily move this' (heavy rock).
Put effects in order from gentle to strong: leaves flutter → branches sway → hard to walk / tree bends.
Answer 'what is wind?' and explain how you know it's windy if you can't see the wind.
Tell a gentle breeze apart from a strong gale and give an example of each.
activities.insight: Checking that wind is moving air known by its effects, that some things move in wind and heavy things resist, and that strength runs along a spectrum from breeze to gale.

activities.title: How do you know it's windy? (talking it through)
steps: Answer a prompt such as 'How do you KNOW it's windy if you can't see the wind? Give me two ways.'
Describe the difference between a gentle breeze and a strong gale in your own words.
Work out, with windows shut indoors, how you could make a little wind yourself.
activities.insight: Articulating that we detect wind only by its effects, and that strength varies, strengthens the observe-by-effects reasoning.

checkQuestion: On a windy day, the branches of a tree are waving about. A child says, 'The trees are making the wind by waving.' Is that right? What is the wind actually, and what's really happening with the trees?
checkAnswer: No — it's the other way round. Wind is moving air. The moving air pushes the branches, which is why they wave; the trees aren't making the wind. We can't see the air itself, but we can see what it does.
